units.title: Ordering at a cafe

lessons.title: Cafe ordering: milk, sugar, sizes and the bill

units.grammarNote: A polite request often starts with אֶפְשָׁר (“is it possible / may I”) plus an infinitive: אֶפְשָׁר לְהַזְמִין, אֶפְשָׁר לִרְאוֹת, אֶפְשָׁר לְשַׁלֵּם. Wants use the gendered present-tense adjective-verb רוֹצֶה (said by a man) / רוֹצָה (said by a woman): the phrasebook stores both under cafe-03. בְּבַקָּשָׁה softens a bare noun into a request (מַיִם קָרִים, בְּבַקָּשָׁה). The object marker אֶת appears before a definite menu: אֶת הַתַּפְרִיט. These notes describe forms already in the phrasebook; they are not a new grammar lesson.

units.title: Asking for and following directions

lessons.title: Directions: streets, corners and 'how do I get to'

units.grammarNote: Location questions use אֵיפֹה (“where”) or אֵיךְ מַגִּיעִים לְ… (“how does one get to…”), the second with an impersonal plural. Movement adverbs already in the phrasebook take a directional ending: יָמִינָה, שְׂמֹאלָה, plus יָשָׁר for “straight.” Imperatives are gendered: לֵךְ / לְכִי, פְּנֵה / פְּנִי, stored on directions-08..10. Close-position phrases are frozen: עַל יַד (next to), מוּל (opposite), בַּפִּנָּה (on the corner). These notes only name forms that are already in the phrasebook and in I-15.

units.title: Shopping and paying

lessons.title: Shuk bargaining: prices, discounts and 'I'll take it'
Supermarket: aisles, prices, bags and the checkout

units.grammarNote: Price questions use כַּמָּה זֶה עוֹלֶה or מָה הַמְּחִיר. אֶפְשָׁר + infinitive makes a polite request (אֶפְשָׁר לִמְדֹּד, אֶפְשָׁר קַבָּלָה, אֶפְשָׁר שַׂקִּית). אֶקַּח אֶת זֶה uses the object marker אֶת before the demonstrative. יֵשׁ / אֵין appear in shop questions (יֵשׁ הַנָּחָה, יֵשׁ לָכֶם). These notes only name forms already in the phrasebook and in il08, il09, I-12 and I-43.

units.title: Transport: taxi, bus and train

lessons.title: Bus and train: tickets, platforms and getting off
Taxi: destination, meter, 'slower' and the receipt

units.grammarNote: Destinations after לְ or לַ are already frozen in the phrasebook (לִשְׂדֵה הַתְּעוּפָה, לַתַּחֲנָה הַמֶּרְכָּזִית, לַמָּלוֹן). אֶפְשָׁר מוֹנֶה is a request for the meter. Which-bus and next-train questions use אֵיזֶה and מָתַי. Gendered “I need” is stored as אֲנִי צָרִיךְ on taxi-01; a feminine form is not in this situation and is held for native review. These notes only name forms already in the phrasebook and in il10, I-11 and I-23.

units.title: Small talk

lessons.title: Small talk: where you're from, how long you've been here, keeping in touch
Work: office, meeting, boss and interview

units.grammarNote: Name questions use מַה שִּׁמְךָ and the impersonal קוֹרְאִים לִי. “Where are you from” is מֵאֵיפֹה אַתָּה (said to a man on small-talk-03); the feminine partner is not in this phrasebook situation and is held for native review. Feeling phrases often put the adjective first: חַם לִי, קַר לִי. These notes only name forms already in the phrasebook and in il13, I-25 and I-36.

units.title: Ordering at a restaurant

lessons.title: Cafe ordering: milk, sugar, sizes and the bill
Dating and going out: asking someone out, plans and compliments

units.grammarNote: The same polite אֶפְשָׁר + infinitive used at a cafe also opens a restaurant request: אֶפְשָׁר לִרְאוֹת אֶת הַתַּפְרִיט, אֶפְשָׁר לְהַזְמִין, אֶפְשָׁר לְשַׁלֵּם בְּכַרְטִיס. Dietary lines are gendered in the phrasebook (אֲנִי צִמְחוֹנִי on cafe-22); the feminine is in I-13, not in this situation’s rows. These notes only name forms already in the phrasebook and in those lessons. ALEF has no separate restaurant phrasebook: every Hebrew line here is copied from the existing cafe situation or cited from those lessons.
